title: Bruno Senna recounts Antonelli’s visit to his family farm
excerpt:
Bruno Senna – former F1 driver and nephew of three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna – has reflected on Kimi Antonelli’s trip to his family’s home, which saw the 20-year-old try out a karting track designed by the legendary Brazilian racer.

Shortly after securing his maiden Drivers’ Championship in Mexico City, Antonelli was invited to the Senna estate and got the chance to sit in the Lotus 98T, the car that Senna raced during the 1986 season.

He also met members of the family as he walked in the footsteps of his racing idol, whom he celebrated with a distinctive yellow and green tribute helmet at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

“We've known that he has been a super fan of Ayrton – and his dad as well, Marco – for a while, and I met him in Imola in 2024,” Senna explained on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid.

“He was there and he was dressed from head to toe in Senna gear. He was doing Formula 2 there, and it was great to meet him. We had a nice chat. It's been so fun to have him be such a supporter.

“We got in touch with him and we offered the opportunity to come to the farm, and we knew that he would enjoy it. We took him around the farm. We took him into the little room where Ayrton did his aeroplane models, and he loved it.

“It was really, really fun to see him. We have the Lotus, the ‘86 car. We had him jump inside the car, and he didn't want to leave the car. You had the turbo boost knob, and he's exploring everything – having an anti-roll bar thing that you can change, and there's a gearstick.

“This is something that was quite funny – I was talking [about] next year when Lotus or McLaren want to do something, we can try to organise for [him] to drive one of these cars because he fits really well in the car.

“You know, his height is perfect for it. His dad was like, ‘I'm not sure if you can drive the manual car’, and Kimi was like, ‘sure I can!’. Finally, we drove on the go-kart track that Ayrton designed.

“It was a really fun thing when I was a kid, and Kimi was incredible. He was so fast, so consistent. We had a fun time. I would say that I was slower because I'm 10kg heavier, but I think there's a bit more than that in it, to be honest! He was amazing.

“The track was very dirty, very full of stone. Kimi was able to create a groove, and he was able to stay within that groove so consistently. It was really impressive. He couldn't move 10cm off because then you don't even run wide – you go onto the grass and spin out because it was so dirty. It was a really cool experience and showed why he's a World Champion.”

Over 30 years on from his untimely death at Imola, Senna is remembered as one of the greatest F1 drivers of all time and continues to motivate different generations – including his nephew, who raced in the sport between 2009 and 2011.

Thinking back to his personal experience on the grid, the younger Senna shared his admiration of Antonelli for maintaining his “humble” approach even whilst fighting for a title.

“When they landed, Marco came out of the helicopter and he had teary eyes because it was something that they never expected,” he said. “Marco was driving when he was younger, and I think he was able to instill this passion, this love for it in Kimi.

“But it also depends on the character of the child to take on this passion. I think Kimi – once he really understood what Ayrton represented as a human being, not only as a racing driver – got really inspired.

Who was Ayrton Senna and why is he regarded as one of F1’s greatest drivers?

“He's incredibly humble, incredibly down to earth. I think it's so easy for your mind to explode when you get into F1. This is a world where you're a god and everybody is [at] your feet, so it's so easy for you to just lose your track.

“I think that it's a difficult trait to be humble and have the right aggression, have the right attitude towards the sport at the same time. I think there are a lot of young drivers who are coming in with a really nice, very natural attitude into F1.

“Gabi [Bortoleto] has a really great heart, Ollie Bearman, Pierre [Gasly]. It makes me really proud of young kids who could be full of themselves, but they stay humble.

“I think this world is a very difficult world, very complicated. I've been here. I know how tricky it is to navigate this paddock, and to have people that are able to still be themselves throughout their F1 careers… For me, it's essential and very pleasing to see.”

To listen to this week’s episode of F1 Beyond The Grid, simply hit go on the audio player above or click here to listen via your preferred podcasting platform.

You can also check out a huge selection of previous episodes – spanning every decade of F1 – in our dedicated F1 Beyond The Grid library.

You can also watch the podcast on the F1 YouTube channel.

title: Where do Mercedes rank among Teams' Championship winners
excerpt:
The Sao Paulo Grand Prix last weekend proved to be a day of celebration for Mercedes, as the German manufacturer secured the 2026 Constructors' Championship.

The Silver Arrows only needed a handful more points than Ferrari to secure the crown in Brazil, which moved Mercedes up to joint third in the all-time Constructors' Championship winners table.

But who remains ahead of them and which other teams have achieved the special accolade?

One-hit wonders

A total of 15 teams have won the Constructors' Championship since it was first introduced in 1958, with six of those managing to secure the title on only one occasion.

The very first was British manufacturer Vanwall during the inaugural season of the new championship standings, with three wins apiece for Stirling Moss and Tony Brooks as the team got the better of Ferrari before the end of the year.

Another British constructor also took the title in 1962, as Graham Hill took the first of his two drivers' titles with the BRM outfit, the combination securing four wins to edge out Jim Clark and Lotus to both titles.

Matra added their name to the list of winners in 1969, the French manufacturer supplying cars to Ken Tyrrell (before creating his own cars for 1970), with Jackie Stewart claiming the first of three drivers' titles.

Stewart's second title came in 1971, and with the help of Francois Cevert, Tyrrell was also able to claim the constructors' title under his own banner.

Nine wins for Michael Schumacher and a further two for team mate Johnny Herbert meant Benetton were able to beat Williams to the teams' crown in 1995, Schumacher also going back-to-back for the drivers' title before moving to Ferrari.

A member of the German's most trusted inner circle at Benetton and then the Scuderia would also add his name to the list of winning constructors, with Ross Brawn taking over Honda's entry for the 2009 season.

Jenson Button's six wins handed him the drivers' title, while two further victories for team mate Rubens Barrichello meant Brawn GP took the title, before morphing into Mercedes for 2010.

Back-to-back champions

Three teams in the history of F1 have only two Constructors' Championships to their name, and all three achieved the feat in back-to-back seasons.

Cooper became the first team, following in the wake of fellow British manufacturer Vanwall by winning the 1959 title with wins for that year's drivers' champion Jack Brabham, as well as Moss and Bruce McLaren.

Brabham secured the second of three drivers' titles the following year with five wins, while another victory for McLaren at the season-opener in Argentina helped Cooper retain their championship.

Having decided to design and build his own cars, in 1966 Brabham became the first, and so far only driver, to win the title racing a car bearing his own name, with the team securing both titles that season.

They achieved the same feat in 1967, but this time Brabham lost out on the drivers' title as team mate Denny Hulme took the accolade.

Despite coming close to title success in the early 1980s, it took until 2005 for Renault to reach the pinnacle of the sport, as Fernando Alonso ensured it was a double success.

The Spaniard and Renault squad, based out of Enstone and becoming what is now the Alpine team, won both titles again the following season in 2006, denying a resurgent Ferrari and Schumacher.

Red Bull (6 titles)

Having taken over the Jaguar outfit for the start of the 2005 season, Red Bull were generally seen by many as nothing more than an energy drinks company trying its hand at racing for a few years.

But under the leadership of Christian Horner and having acquired the services of design guru Adrian Newey from McLaren, the team began to make waves and claimed their first wins in 2009 as Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber achieved six between them over the course of the campaign.

The duo then did enough to claim the team's first title the following season, with Vettel also winning the drivers' title in dramatic circumstances at an Abu Dhabi showdown.

That began a run of dominance as four double titles went the way of Red Bull and Vettel until the 2013 season, the team securing 41 wins with the German and Webber over that period.

New power unit changes for 2014 put Red Bull on the back foot, and despite occasional wins for Daniel Ricciardo and Max Verstappen, it wasn't until 2021 that the latter was able to have a title tilt for the first time.

Like Vettel, Verstappen went on a run of four consecutive titles, and with the help of team mate Sergio Perez, Red Bull also came away with two more titles in 2022 and 2023.

Lotus (7 titles)

Such was the dominance of Lotus under the leadership of team owner and designer Colin Chapman during the 1960s and 1970s, that the British manufacturer still remains fifth on this list.

Chapman's first title came in 1963 as he and Clark became one of the sport's greatest pairings, the Scot also taking that year's title as the combination did the double again in 1965.

Even Clark's death early in 1968 during an F2 race at Hockenheim couldn't prevent Chapman from another title double, this time with Hill taking his second drivers' title.

There was further tragedy just two years later, with Jochen Rindt securing the 1970 crown posthumously after his death in practice at Monza after five wins that season, with F1 rookie Emerson Fittipaldi winning in the US on just his fourth start to help secure the teams' title.

Fittipaldi would lead the team to the double again in 1972 at the wheel of the Lotus 72, with the Brazilian and team mate Ronnie Peterson claiming another crown for Lotus the following year, although both missed out on the drivers' title to Stewart.

Lotus and Chapman's final championship success came in 1978, the legendary designer creating the Lotus 79 with its ground effect aerodynamics, allowing Mario Andretti to also claim the drivers' title, although the success was overshadowed by the death of Peterson at Monza.

Although the team remained in F1 well into the 1990s even after Chapman's death in 1982, and achieved further victories with the likes of Elio de Angelis and Ayrton Senna, they never again claimed another title success.

Williams (9 titles)

Although Williams' last title came in 1997, they still remain joint third on the list.

The collaboration of team owner Frank Williams, designer Patrick Head and the no-nonsense approach of Alan Jones proved incredibly effective, and after wins in 1979, the first title followed in 1980 for both car and driver.

Although Jones and team mate Carlos Reutemann, missed out on the drivers' title the following season, the teams' title still went to Williams after the pair achieved two wins apiece.

Despite a drivers' title for Keke Rosberg in 1982, it took until 1986 for Williams to become the dominant force in F1 again with Honda engines, as they secured back-to-back teams' titles, along with the drivers' crown for Nelson Piquet in 1987.

Losing Honda power dropped the team down the pecking order, before a new collaboration with Renault brought their most prosperous period to date at the start of the 1990s.

Nigel Mansell finally secured his long-awaited title in 1992 as Williams dominated, with the team achieving both titles again in 1993 with Alain Prost leading the team.

Senna's death at the start of the 1994 season meant Damon Hill became Schumacher's main challenger, and although the Briton missed out on the individual crown, he along with Mansell and David Coulthard helped Williams secure another title.

Hill and Williams were finally on top in 1996, before Jacques Villeneuve secured the double again in 1997, which remains the team's final championship success to date.

Mercedes (9 titles)

Mercedes dominated F1 in 1955 with Juan Manuel Fangio and Stirling Moss, the former claiming that year's drivers' title, before the Silver Arrows left the sport for more than five decades.

Having taken over Brawn's outfit for the start of the 2010 season, it took until 2014 and an overhaul in power unit regulations before the team were back to winning ways.

But once they started winning, it was hard for the German manufacturer to stop as they claimed eight teams' titles between 2014 and 2021.

Those first three seasons saw Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg battle for the title, with the German finally claiming the sport's biggest prize in 2016 before retiring.

That opened the door for Valtteri Bottas to join the team, and although not as serious a title threat to Hamilton, the Finn ensured that Mercedes claimed another five teams' titles on the bounce, including in 2021 when Hamilton lost out on the drivers' title to Verstappen.

By that point Verstappen and Red Bull had become the dominant force in F1, and it took until another ruleset change at the beginning of 2026 for Mercedes to move back to the very front of the grid.

Kimi Antonelli became the youngest World Champion in F1 history at the Mexico City Grand Prix, while just a week later in Sao Paulo, Mercedes were once again back on top.

McLaren (10 wins)

Bruce McLaren's eponymous team continued even after his death during a testing accident at Goodwood in 1970, going on to become one of the most successful in F1.

The first of 10 teams' titles came in 1974, as Fittipaldi also claimed his second drivers' title, but it took another 10 years before McLaren had a driver combination to claim the constructors' accolade.

They found it in the shape of Niki Lauda and Prost, the pair separated by only half a point at the end of the 1984 season, before the latter went on a run of three consecutive titles – with McLaren claiming the teams' title in 1985.

With Senna joining McLaren for 1988, the combination became almost unbeatable as the team secured 15 out of 16 race wins that year, Senna just beating Prost to the title.

With Prost leaving for Ferrari, Senna and new team mate Gerhard Berger secured more titles across 1990 and 1991 before McLaren slipped down the pecking order.

It wasn't until 1998 when Mika Hakkinen, with the aid of Mercedes power, returned the team to the top after beating Schumacher and Ferrari, and although the Finn won again in 1999, McLaren missed out.

It took until 2024 for McLaren to reach the top again as a constructor, with Mercedes power once again helping Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to victories, which culminated in the former winning the drivers' title in 2025 as McLaren defended their teams' crown.

Ferrari (16 titles)

Having been in F1 since the creation of the championship back in 1950, it's perhaps unsurprising that Ferrari should be top of this list.

The Scuderia got their first taste of title success as a manufacturer in 1961 as American Phil Hill won the drivers' title, which was followed three years later by another double, this time with John Surtees at the wheel.

Lauda's move in 1974 galvanised the team, and the following year they secured three teams' titles in succession with the Austrian also earning the drivers' crown in 1975 and 1977 – having returned from his fiery shunt and narrowly missing out in 1976.

Jody Scheckter and Gilles Villeneuve led the team to another brace of titles in 1979, the former claiming the drivers' title, before back-to-back team titles came in 1982 and 1983 as Didier Pironi, Rene Arnoux and Patrick Tambay all won races for the team.

It took until the late 1990s and Schumacher's influence to earn the Scuderia another title, which came in 1999 as a broken leg for the German opened the door for Eddie Irvine to challenge Hakkinen for the title.

Fully recovered for the start of the new decade, Schumacher and Ferrari became the dominant force in F1, claiming five consecutive drivers' and teams' titles.

With Schumacher retiring at the end of 2006, Kimi Raikkonen joined Felipe Massa at the team, the pair helping Ferrari to another title as the Finn ultimately claimed the drivers' title.

Although Massa just missed out on a drivers' title of his own to Hamilton the following season in the most dramatic circumstances, he and Raikkonen did enough to earn Ferrari a 16th title – currently the most recent it has achieved.

title: Bearman relieved ‘horrible three weeks’ for Haas are over
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman finished 17th in Sao Paulo last Sunday and afterwards cut a despondent figure as he revealed how pleased he was to be heading home after a tough triple header.

Bearman failed to finish the races in Austin and Mexico City, while his Sao Paulo Grand Prix unravelled thanks to some slow pit stops that dropped him from the fringes of the points to towards the back of the field.

Having put in a superb lap in the wet to qualify in the top 10, nothing in the Grand Prix quite went to plan for the Haas man, starting with early contact with Fernando Alonso that sent both drivers wide after a handful of corners.

“I had a bit of a moment at the start but nothing major, I lost a few places at the start but managed to gain back a few again, so was net zero,” he explained. “After that I just had some very slow pit stops and I couldn’t fight with that.”

That pit stop dropped him from P10 to P17 on a day where points felt possible, with the rain causing havoc and plenty of strategic dilemmas to contend with. Anyone who got those strategy calls right could have climbed up the order – as shown by Nico Hulkenberg managing to finish P10 despite serving a 10-second time penalty.

“I just want to go home and reset. It has been a horrible three weeks, we have missed two opportunities to score points, and we just need to move on and do better,” Bearman concluded.

His triple header started with problems in Austin when he made contact with Pierre Gasly when fighting for position. That earned him a 10-second time penalty for causing a collision, which combined with the resultant damage forced his retirement.

“I sent one up the inside, and to be honest, he saw me as he left space but to me, it didn’t feel enough. He gave space, but only half a car's worth, and I was committed, so we made a bit of contact – I picked up a huge amount of damage on my car, and I probably damaged his car as well,” was what Bearman said at the time.

Camara experiences every condition in 'tricky' Haas debut

"It was a shame as I felt like I was massively penalised anyway, as the damage ruined my race, and on top of that I picked up the penalty. In my view, it was a racing incident.”

Worse was to come in Mexico City, when he was hit from behind by Hulkenberg, forcing another retirement with damage.

On a day where so many post-race penalties were handed out, Bearman lost the opportunity to score – with his stand-in team mate Ryo Hirakawa promoted to P10 from his 13th place finish.

“I just got smashed off. I was turning into Turn 4, and the next thing I knew, I was looking at everyone else coming past me, facing the wrong way,” Bearman said of the moment.

“It was a good race to be honest, I had great pace, and we were in the fight for points, and I was in the points when I was taken out. It happens, it just sucks.”

As a result of all that, it is easy to see why Bearman is keen to go home, with Haas scoring just the one point in the last three-race run, while rivals Audi managed to pick up five points to close the gap in the standings in the fight for seventh.

Haas remain in front, but only by three points with three rounds remaining.

title: ‘He was immediately fast’ – Antonelli’s junior racing boss on his early potential
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli’s ascent to Formula 1 World Champion has been meteoric, coming in only his second season in the sport, and at an age where most drivers are typically striving to graduate from junior categories.

The young Italian spent only three-and-a-half years on the FIA single seater pyramid, but was with the legendary PREMA outfit every step of the way. We sat down with PREMA’s former head honcho Rene Rosin to reflect on Antonelli’s remarkable rise.

Until 2026, the Rosin family operated the highly successful PREMA team that competed across junior motorsport, and it was with them that Antonelli worked his way up the ladder before landing a seat at Mercedes.

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Sao Paulo?
excerpt:
The first race of 2026 without a Mercedes driver on the podium was ironically where the team clinched the Constructors’ Championship, with Lando Norris and the Red Bull pair denying them a spot in the top three in Sao Paulo. But who impressed our Power Rankings judges? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below…

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

With other teams switching their resources to 2027, McLaren were the only ones to bring upgrades to Interlagos, but Norris was cautious of anticipating any major improvement. While it’s difficult to say just how much they helped considering the way the weather jumbled up the pecking order, Norris’ skill in the wet was clear as he converted pole position to his third triumph of the season. One of the main factors that contributed to his 14s winning margin was, in his words, an ability to keep it cool and avoid mistakes.

Was it really a Sao Paulo Grand Prix if Max Verstappen didn’t charge from the back of the field to the podium? After his stellar comeback drives in 2024 and 2025, he pulled off another by climbing from P21 to P5 during his opening stint on the intermediate tyres. The softs weren’t as good to him, but he caught his team mate to improve to second place and simultaneously take a stronger grip of P2 in the drivers’ standings.

Liam Lawson was arguably the biggest winner of the Qualifying chaos at the rain-soaked Interlagos, with his original result of P5 becoming P3 once the final order had shaken out. He made the most of it too, joining Kimi Antonelli in storming past Norris on the opening lap, but was passed by the top teams as the race progressed. Nevertheless, his admirable defence against Charles Leclerc paid off when the latter was handed a five-second time penalty for making contact in their wheel-to-wheel contest, elevating Lawson to P7 post-race.

Although Isack Hadjar hasn’t been satisfied with the handling of his RB22 in recent rounds, he seemed to turn a corner in Sao Paulo as he excelled in the challenging conditions. Starting fifth, he had the opposite experience to Verstappen and performed best on the soft tyres, getting stuck into several thrilling battles with Antonelli en route to finishing on the podium for the first time since the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Interlagos is where Fernando Alonso secured both of his Drivers’ Championships, and two decades later, he still goes well there. The Spaniard delivered Aston Martin’s first Q3 appearance of the season before tackling a tantalising fight with Alex Albon, which saw him pounce when the Williams driver drifted wide. He still lacked that little bit extra to break into the points, bringing home a respectable P12.

Wet weather always opens up opportunities for the midfield, and the Sao Paulo Grand Prix was no exception. A strong Qualifying led to Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg lining up on the second row, but he didn’t get the launch he needed and immediately lost positions. While that left him scrapping with Franco Colapinto at the fringes of the points, a 10-second time penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage appeared to rule the German out of top-10 contention. However, the late rain played into his hands and he overtook Arvid Lindblad for P10.

A power unit issue cut Lindblad’s Qualifying session short and prompted Racing Bulls to replace his internal combustion engine and turbocharger, resulting in another grid penalty. It would’ve been easy to forget that he started from P18 as he quickly surged through the field, challenging the likes of Alonso and Hulkenberg throughout, although he was unable to hold off the Audi man for P10 over the final laps.

Undaunted by his grid penalty, Lewis Hamilton gained an astonishing 11 positions at the start – and for a few laps, it looked as though he could produce a Verstappen-style comeback to challenge for the podium. However, his tyres rapidly faded and he tumbled back down the order, so it was no surprise that he wanted to gamble by being the first to pit for slicks. He enjoyed another boost by doing just that, but his race unravelled when the rain returned, with a spin and late stop limiting him to P9.

Although a five-place grid penalty meant that it was impossible for George Russell to start on pole, he was still furious when the team’s call to abandon his second Q3 lap left him to qualify behind Norris and subsequently drop to P7. He made good progress on the inters before losing any advantage he had when he switched to slicks, as shown by his unusual spin at the pit exit. After that, the pace gradually came back to him and he passed Antonelli for P4 – his best finish since winning in Baku.

“Extremely disappointed,” was Antonelli’s verdict of his performance at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, with the Italian much more content to focus on Mercedes’ overall victory as a team. His initial launch saw him snatch the lead from Norris and build a commanding gap, but like Russell, his race unravelled on the soft tyres. A lack of grip caused Antonelli to spin at Turn 1 and let Norris back through, and he lost out further when the rain fell later on, leaving him to settle for P5.

Missing out

Just missing out on this week’s Power Rankings leaderboard are Haas' Ollie Bearman (17th, after contact with Alonso, slow pit stops and a penalty for an unsafe release) and Williams' Albon (15th, after losing pace when the track dried out).

title: F1 ACADEMY announces 2027 calendar
excerpt:
F1 ACADEMY has revealed its calendar for the 2027 campaign, with the all-female series’ fifth season featuring seven rounds.

The series will continue to support Formula 1 across rounds in Asia, Europe and North America next year.

The 2027 campaign will commence at the Jeddah Corniche Circuit in Saudi Arabia in March, before heading to Shanghai in April and Montreal’s Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve a month later.

A European double-header kicks off with a visit to Silverstone on July 2-4. The series then heads to Budapest for the first time, with the Hungaroring becoming the 17th circuit to feature an F1 ACADEMY round on July 30 – August 1.

F1 ACADEMY returns to action with two trips to the United States, racing around the Circuit of The Americas in Austin in late October. The 2027 season will once again draw to a close under the bright lights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit in November.

DateVenueMarch 19-21Jeddah Corniche Circuit, Saudi ArabiaApril 16-18Shanghai International Circuit, ChinaMay 21-23Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, CanadaJuly 2-4Silverstone Circuit, Great BritainJuly 30 – August 1Hungaroring, HungaryOctober 22-24Circuit of The Americas, United StatesNovember 18-20Las Vegas Strip Circuit, United States

Susie Wolff, Managing Director of F1 ACADEMY, said: “It’s hard to believe we’re already heading into our fifth season of F1 ACADEMY. What we’ve collectively achieved in such a short space of time is something we can all be proud of, and I’m equally excited about what lies ahead.

“With our 2027 calendar, we’re continuing to build consistency in where we race, which is important for our drivers, teams and fans. I’m hugely grateful to our promoters for their continued support and belief in what we’re building.

“Every season we’re seeing more fans, more young girls inspired to get involved in motorsport and more opportunities for female talent. The level of competition continues to rise year on year, and we’ve seen some incredible racing as a result. I’m excited to see that level pushed even higher in 2027.”

title: Camara experiences every condition in ‘tricky’ Haas debut
excerpt:
While Rafael Camara saw the chequered flag in a “tricky” debut race for Haas last weekend, the Brazilian faced with the tough task of navigating his first Grand Prix on home soil and in changeable conditions.

The F2 star had already been announced as one of Haas’ drivers for next season, but when the team opted not to field Esteban Ocon, Camara was given the opportunity to make his debut ahead of schedule.

He was able to take part in all three practice sessions to try and find his way with the VF-26, but those were completed in the dry – Qualifying was another matter. The heavens opened, the track was red flagged and Camara was faced with some of the most difficult conditions in recent memory.

He hit the barriers in Q1, had the composure to get back to the pits with a broken front wing, and the guts to go back out and stick another lap in – which was good enough for Q2. But then the rookie crashed out at the end of that segment, locking up and going straight into the barriers.

“I was just a bit unlucky in the last corner, locking up, and then trying to make the corner, but it was really not possible," was his mature take on how Saturday had gone.

"In a way, I’m a bit disappointed with the mistakes, as I know for the team, that’s not what they want, but overall I think it was a positive session.”

With rain falling again on Sunday, conditions were not getting any easier for Camara, who started 11th thanks to grid penalties for some ahead. He lost ground off the line and skated wide again, but was able to keep going and finished in 20th place.

“It definitely wasn’t an easy one, with all the conditions out there we experienced over the course of one race. In the beginning, it was about staying on track, and there were a couple of mistakes – it was a bit tricky,” he admitted.

5 Winners and 5 Losers from Sao Paulo

“The positive is that there was no damage today and lots learned, but there’s still a lot more to learn for the future. I think there are a lot of things to go through with the team and put in place for next time.

“On one side, I was trying to enjoy my first race in Formula 1, at home, so it was nice – but I think on my side, I wasn’t fully satisfied with how we finished today. It was a weekend where I think I must’ve nearly experienced everything, so I’ve learned a lot for the future.”

Ollie Bearman in the other Haas car started in the top 10 and came home in 17th after a slow pit stop, so both drivers went backwards in Brazil on a tough day that saw Audi close to within three points of the American outfit in the fight for seventh in the constructors’ battle.

Given the Brazilian finished at Interlagos, experiencing a drying track, the crossover between intermediate and slick tyres and then the pitfalls of slithering back to the pits for more inters as the rain fell, he has ticked a fair few boxes on debut, and impressed people in the paddock.

"I had a look [on Saturday], until the last corner, he did a mega lap at the beginning of the Quali, and this lap would have been a super lap," Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur said of Camara's performance.

"But honestly, to start in F1, when it's your home race, you have these kind of conditions, that you have to put in inter, medium, soft... It's wet during Quali and the same [in the] race, mega cold conditions today, it was probably the most difficult weekend that he could have had, but he's doing very well. The pace was impressive yesterday."

Haas boss Ayao Komatsu agreed: "He made some mistakes, but overall, I think they were very challenging conditions to make your debut, so well done to him for completing this race without any big issues. We know he has performance, he has speed, it’s just about consistency and delivering it."

title: Why McLaren went the opposite way to Mercedes' front wing
excerpt:
Just underscoring the idea that what works for one car won’t necessarily be good for another, McLaren have made precisely the opposite change in their front wing philosophy to that recently made by Mercedes.

The new McLaren wing in Sao Paulo is joined to the nose via the middle of the three elements rather than the bottom element used previously. Mercedes made the opposite change at the recent US Grand Prix.

title: Mick Schumacher makes surgery decision after year-long painful injury
excerpt:
Mick Schumacher raced the entirety of the 2026 IndyCar season with an injured wrist.

Mick Schumacher will head into his second IndyCar campaign without going under the knife, choosing to manage his left wrist problem through conservative treatment and physiotherapy rather than surgery.

The German, who has swapped Rahal Letterman Lanigan Racing for Meyer Shank Racing for the 2027 season, has been carrying the issue since the opening round of the year in St. Petersburg.

A chain-reaction crash triggered by Sting Ray Robb in the early stages of that race saw the steering wheel snap back violently, chipping a small bone fragment in Schumacher's wrist.

Surgery looked likely at several points across the campaign, but Schumacher and his medical team have now decided to delay any operation.

"The most important thing is really to avoid surgery," Schumacher explained, as quoted by Motorsport.com.

"So we've done a lot of physiotherapy and worked intensively to get it under control. After several MRIs, we came to the conclusion that it's better to go another year without surgery."

Mick Schumacher aware future operation is possible

How much the wrist bothers him in the cockpit depends heavily on how the car behaves. On circuits that reward smooth steering inputs, the symptoms are barely noticeable.

"Everything that is gentle on the hand is completely normal and totally fine," said Schumacher.

"The fast, jerky movements are the ones that usually hurt the wrist. I felt it most intensely when the rear was relatively loose."

That dynamic may explain why some of Schumacher's strongest results as a rookie came on ovals, where smooth, measured inputs are required rather than abrupt corrections.

Across the six oval rounds at Phoenix, Indianapolis, St. Louis, Nashville and Milwaukee, he picked up 97 points, qualified P4 at both Phoenix and Milwaukee, and was named Indianapolis 500 Rookie of the Year.

Surgery remains an option further down the line should the wrist worsen during the 2027 season, but for now Schumacher's focus is on settling in at Meyer Shank Racing.

"We'll just see next year whether it stays good or not," he said. "If it gets worse, we'll have to operate then."

title: Max Verstappen handed Mercedes warning in 'egotistical' Lewis Hamilton take down
excerpt:
Ralf Schumacher has explained why he believes Max Verstappen and Mercedes would not work, whilst also taking aim at Lewis Hamilton's leadership skills.

Ralf Schumacher has questioned whether Max Verstappen would be a good fit for Mercedes, suggesting the Dutchman's hands-on approach could create difficulties within the team.

The former F1 driver also criticised Lewis Hamilton's leadership qualities, arguing the seven-time world champion has never learned how to lead a team during his spells at McLaren and Mercedes.

Verstappen has committed his long-term future to Red Bull after signing a contract extension until the end of 2030, extending his association with the Milton Keynes-based outfit.

The four-time F1 world champion has established himself as a central figure at Red Bull, but Schumacher believes his level of technical involvement could make a potential switch to Mercedes difficult.

Speaking on Sky Sport Germany's F1 podcast, Backstage Boxengasse, Schumacher suggested Verstappen's working relationship with Red Bull would not necessarily translate to another team.

"I think that would be very difficult," Schumacher said. "Max is used to [something different]... He's so technically switched on, he wants to know exactly what's going on.

"He basically gets in the car and wants to know straight away what's happening with the gearbox, with the differential. Or how a damper works, for example. He'd find it interesting to dig into that regardless."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Schumacher questions Hamilton leadership

Schumacher's assessment of Verstappen came as he discussed the different dynamics within F1 teams, including the situation facing Hamilton at Ferrari.

The German questioned whether Hamilton possesses the leadership qualities required to shape a team around him, suggesting his previous experiences under Ron Dennis at McLaren and Toto Wolff at Mercedes had not prepared him for such a role.

His comments followed Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur's call for his drivers to show greater respect for the team following a clash between Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Schumacher believes Hamilton's career has largely centred on extracting the maximum performance from the car rather than taking responsibility for the wider team.

"Hamilton never learned how to lead a team, not under Toto Wolff and not under Ron Dennis," Schumacher stated. "That was never his job anyway. He just had to get in the car and drive as fast as possible.

"I think you can see that, and I think it's made him quite egotistical as well."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Schumacher highlights key Verstappen difference

In contrast, Schumacher believes Verstappen's upbringing has played a significant role in shaping his technical approach, pointing to the influence of his father, former F1 driver Jos Verstappen.

The German compared that background to his own experiences growing up alongside his brother, seven-time world champion Michael Schumacher.

"And Max is also from the generation that grew up with his father, who worked on cars himself, just like it was with me and my brother," Schumacher explained.

"I think that's the big difference."

Schumacher also questioned whether Mercedes would welcome the level of influence Verstappen has developed at Red Bull, suggesting the established structure of the Brackley-based outfit could prove an obstacle.

He believes Ferrari, by contrast, is more accustomed to accommodating significant demands from its drivers, partly because of the legacy left by Michael Schumacher.

"Who did he grow up with, after all? Together with Red Bull. Mercedes is already a big team. If someone like Max went there now, I don't think they'd be too keen on that.

"At Ferrari, I think they're used to a driver being able to make demands, but in my opinion that still comes from Michael [Schumacher], from what he left behind there."

title: Aston Martin highlight painful disparity after 'unfortunate takeaway'
excerpt:
Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack has pointed out a crippling contrast at the Silverstone-based squad, after Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll suffered three retirements out of six starts in F1's most recent triple-header.

The performance of the AMR26 was more convincing at the São Paulo Grand Prix, with Alonso even able to mix it with the Ferraris in the tricky conditions at Interlagos.

Having qualified an impressive ninth on the grid and starting eighth, the two-time F1 drivers' champion was, however, unable to stay in the points, ultimately falling to P12 as his team-mate retired for the 13th time in 20 rounds.

The Spaniard failing to add to his haul of seven points this season was, to Krack, the main "takeaway" of the weekend in Brazil, despite encouraging signs from the car.

"When the conditions were difficult, like [in qualifying], and also like [the race], I think the competitiveness was better; it was improved," Krack told media, including RacingNews365.

"And especially [in the race], it was a good performance considering the overall picture of the year. It was one of the most competitive weekends.

"So, unfortunately, no points. That is always the takeaway of a weekend."

[Article continues below]

The positives and negatives

With Aston Martin still plagued with reliability issues emanating from the Honda power unit, Krack was keen to emphasise the conflicting conclusions that can be drawn from the round at Interlagos.

"All in all, we have beaten some competitors that are faster than us, certainly faster cars," he added.

"So, a positive from that point of view, but also, if you review the last triple header, we had five [three] DNFs out of six races.

"That is something we certainly need to work on. So, positive from the competitiveness side, but not so positive from reliability."

title: Unusual Toto Wolff method hailed for helping Mercedes through 'extremely tough times'
excerpt:
George Russell has praised the leadership of Toto Wolff, highlighting how Mercedes did not resort to a hiring-and-firing culture during the team's relatively lean period.

Having secured eight consecutive constructors' championships between 2014 and 2021, the Silver Arrows went titleless through the contemporary ground effect era, which covered the past four seasons.

Despite finishing second twice in that span, the Wolff-led team was never in contention for the championship, and only amassed seven victories.

However, with F1 ushering in a new generation of cars in 2026, the Brackley-based squad has returned to the summit, wrapping up its ninth constructors' crown at the São Paulo Grand Prix.

Whereas other sports teams may have cleared house to fully rebuild, Mercedes limited turnover in key staff, which Russell, who is fighting for second in the F1 drivers' standings after team-mate Kimi Antonelli won the title, was keen to point out.

"We have been through a lot over those years. It's been extremely tough times," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

"But I think something I admire a lot about Toto's leadership is that the people we have today are the same people who were there during the glory years, and they're the same people who went through the difficulties during 2022 to 2025. Nobody was hired or fired."

Russell elaborated, heralding the three central pillars of Wolff's leadership that paved the way for the team to emerge victorious again.

"The trust and belief stayed with the core group of people, and now we've come through...," the eight-time grand prix added.

Credit to everybody in the team, but huge credit to Toto for that loyalty and belief in the people, even when times were tough."

title: Valtteri Bottas responds to Colton Herta breaking crucial threshold to race in F1
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas has addressed Colton Herta finally securing his FIA Super Licence, a milestone the American reached during opening practice at the São Paulo Grand Prix, with his Cadillac seat under threat from the development.

Herta needed to accumulate 40 Super Licence points over a rolling three-year period to be eligible to race in Formula 1, and Cadillac went to considerable lengths to get him there.

The 26-year-old was entered in Formula 2 with Hitech this year and also ran across six separate FP1 sessions, all in pursuit of the points he was missing.

It has not been straightforward. In addition to an underwhelming campaign in F2 that will not contribute to his tally, an error on IndyCar's official website complicated the process, listing Herta sixth rather than seventh in the 2025 standings.

That miscalculation led Cadillac and Herta to believe he had already reached 40 points at the Mexico City Grand Prix, only for the corrected classification to leave him one short.

And a hydraulic issue that limited him to five laps during Monza practice earlier in the season, short of the 100-kilometre minimum needed to bank a point.

But Herta eventually got over the line in FP1 in Brazil, completing more than 100 clean kilometres in Sergio Perez's MAC-26.

Bottas, on the other hand, has struggled to match the Mexican's pace this year with numerous unconvincing performances and a spate of bad luck, including his scary suspension failure in Mexico City and his DNS due to a cross-threaded wheel nut at Interlagos.

Asked how he felt about the situation given the effort invested in getting Herta over the line, the Finnish driver told media, including RacingNews365: "Normally, nothing should change for the future.

"But there's obviously been good effort on giving him the super licence."

Bottas highlighted how there is an element of urgency in getting Herta over the line, as 30 of his super licence points came in 2024, when he finished second in the IndyCar championship.

"I can understand it; it's now or never for him to get the licence," the 10-time grand prix winner added. "But for the future, I don't know."

title: 'Savage' Max Verstappen handed 'outrageous' appraisal after Lando Norris hunt
excerpt:
Max Verstappen almost performed what many thought was impossible in Brazil.

James Hinchcliffe has delivered an "outrageous" verdict on Max Verstappen's charge through the field at the São Paulo Grand Prix, branding the Red Bull driver a "savage competitor" after he carved his way from the back of the grid to finish second behind race winner Lando Norris.

Verstappen started from 21st on the grid after taking an engine-related penalty for exceeding his season's power unit component allocation.

He crossed the line just 14.602 seconds behind Norris, who converted pole position into victory despite a wheelspin issue off the line.

Speaking on the F1 Nation podcast, Hinchcliffe pointed out that Verstappen's run to the podium from the back has become a habit at Interlagos.

"You have one little issue, a mechanical issue on Lando's car, and he's won the race from 21st on the grid," Hinchcliffe said on the F1 Nation podcast. "I mean, it's outrageous.

"The challenge with Max is that we're not sure how he would do if he got the chance to start up front because he hasn't done it here in so long.

"That's three years in a row now that he's had to do starts from the teens, pit lane or the 20s, and all three times he's ended up on the podium. So it's remarkable what he's accomplished at this track over the last few years."

Driver

Max Verstappen

Dutch

3

Max Verstappen playing Lando Norris mind games

Verstappen suggested after the race that he could have closed in further on Norris had his grid penalty not pushed him to the back, a claim Hinchcliffe said was a calculated piece of gamesmanship.

Discussing Verstappen implying he would have been closer to Norris had he not started from the back, Hinchcliffe said: "And that's exactly what you should say to get into the head of your competition, right? Lando won this race by 10 seconds last year, and on the cool-down lap, he said it wasn't a big enough margin.

"Well, he did it by 14 this year, but Max is going to be the first to be like, 'Well, yeah, it was 14, but was it?' But that's also what makes him such a fierce competitor. He can have a drive like that but still be picking apart what went wrong.

"And for all we know, they'll bring that car back to the factory or to the next race, pull it apart and find maybe something broke or something wasn't quite right. Very possible. These cars are very complicated and complex, but that's why, again, he's such a savage competitor that, even after a drive like that, he's still trying to figure out how he could be better."

title: F1 drivers air frustrations after 'speed limit' introduction
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad and Gabriel Bortoleto have voiced frustration with the "speed limit" placed on F1 cars during the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

For the new 2026 power unit regulations, the cars normally churn out 350kw of electrical energy, with this making up around 50% of the total power output.

However, for safety reasons, in wet weather conditions, the output is capped at 250kw - a reduction of 100kw - to ensure drivers are able to keep the cars under control and not go spinning off.

This means that whilst cars are able to drive freely in clean air, once they try to attempt to pass a rival, they can hit a block in terms of power as the cap is reached, and energy harvesting then begins.

For Lindblad, who was trying to fight his way back into the points following his second change to slick soft tyres, this proved troublesome, as he came up behind the Alpine of Franco Colapinto whilst trying to battle Nico Hulkenberg's Audi for the final point in 10th - something the German ultimately hung on to - despite serving a 10-second time penalty.

"It was a hard fight, and I had a speed limiter with the energy," Lindblad said of his battle with Colapinto to media, including RacingNews365.

"So that was nice with the way it works.

"So I used the boost, and then he goes faster than me at the end of the straight, which is amazing, with the overtake mode."

Further discussing his race, the rookie then described how it had fallen apart in the closing laps as he tumbled from the points - having been running as high as eighth on Lap 45 before the second stop for a set of new softs put him behind Hulkenberg and Colapinto.

"It was a fun race, I enjoyed it a lot, especially if it ended on Lap 50 or 55, as we need to see what happened in the last 15, 20 laps as I don't think we managed everything perfectly," he said

"I obviously lost a lot of time with Franco, and I don't know if we could have made better decisions or if we were unlucky with the timing to go to the wet tyres - and unfortunately, I had big drivability problems in the last 10 laps, so it was incredibly difficult to race Nico.

"It was just about keeping the car on track, and it is a shame, because with 15 laps to go, in my head, we were going to be in the points - so I don't see where it went wrong."

[Article continues below]

Bortoleto's point of view

As for Bortoleto, his weekend was all but over in qualifying after he spun off at Juncao in Q1 and made to start 19th, after penalties for Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton, and Sergio Perez.

He recovered to 16th place, albeit aided by the Did Not Start of Valtteri Bottas and Lance Stroll's retirement.

The home driver spoke of how as soon as he escaped traffic, the "clean air" was not a problem with the 250kw limit.

"I mean, I got stuck, and it was difficult to overtake because we're limited to 250kw on the straights," Bortoleto added.

"So it was difficult to make a really big gap, but as soon as I got clean air, I was very quick, but that doesn't matter at the end of the day, because you are starting from the back.

"So we are just saying what could have been, but it was not. The only thing I can do is learn from my mistake in qualifying and move to the next race."

title: Max Verstappen given 'an extra point' for 'simply sensational' reason
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has been awarded an "11 out of 10" by former F1 driver Christian Danner for mastering a poorly handling Red Bull during the São Paulo Grand Prix.

Verstappen charged from 21st on the grid to finish second behind Lando Norris at Interlagos, having taken a power unit penalty.

The Dutchman made rapid progress in the wet conditions but encountered extreme oversteer after switching to slick tyres, before his RB22's balance changed dramatically again when he returned to intermediates.

Danner, who won the inaugural Formula 3000 championship in 1985 before racing in F1 for Zakspeed, Osella, Arrows and Rial, was particularly impressed by Verstappen's racecraft.

"I saw the grand prix, of course, and I actually thought a lot about it because there were a few things over the weekend that impressed me and pleased me a lot. And, of course, Max's performance was one of the things that I thoroughly enjoyed," Danner told Lottoland Live Casino.

"He did extremely well, and his ability in classic racing things, you know, wheel-to-wheel racing, overtaking, choosing maybe a slightly different line, that is his speciality, and he's an absolute master at doing that.

"However, I give him an extra point. You know, he gets 10 out of 10 anyway, so I give him an 11 out of 10 for the fact that the car didn't really handle very well, which was clearly not to his liking. And the way he mastered it was simply sensational, I have to say.

"And what the hell went wrong with that thing, I don't know, but the handling was poor. And therefore, you know, a drive like that means an awful lot."

Danner also welcomed the FIA's decision to allow racing in the rain.

"However, what I enjoyed most was the fact that the FIA race director decided to let them go out in the bloody rain, and everybody was on [intermediate] tyres," he added. "And as a tremendous surprise to everybody, it worked out."

title: Ferrari doomed by painful compromise in São Paulo GP debacle
excerpt:
Ferrari had to compensate for its lack of power unit performance at Interlagos. RacingNews365 technical analyst Paolo Filisetti explains how that compromise plagued the Scuderia's entire weekend.

Ferrari's performance in the São Paulo Grand Prix fell well short of the level shown a week earlier in Mexico City, and indeed of previous rounds, with the characteristics of Interlagos proving to be the worst possible conditions for the SF-26.

The circuit's heavily twisting middle sector, combined with a quick final sector, created a difficult combination for the car.

To compensate for its draggy nature, Ferrari's engineers opted for a relatively low-downforce aerodynamic setup, which proved wholly inadequate through the middle sector, leaving the car understeering with a rear end that was extremely snappy.

It was clear from first practice that the weekend would not replicate the competitiveness seen in Mexico, where the thinner air had actually played to the strengths of the car's aerodynamics while also bringing out the best in Maranello's power unit.

The smaller-diameter turbine of the Scuderia's power unit had sharply reduced turbo lag at 2,240 metres of altitude, a factor that simply did not apply at sea level in Brazil.

A car set up around a compromise

The SF-26 is not a flawed design. Its strong aerodynamic and chassis characteristics can only partially mask the shortfall in power from the engine, however.

Had Ferrari possessed a more powerful engine in Brazil, the aerodynamic setup would likely have leaned towards more downforce, a configuration that would have been decisive through the circuit's mixed middle sector and made the car more competitive overall. As it stood, the compromise left little room to manoeuvre.

The weather added another complication. Rain reduced grip to the point where intermediate tyres were required, but it was the low temperatures that caused the bigger headache, narrowing the tyres' effective working window.

[Article continues below]

Tyre pressures and a backfiring call

It has emerged that Ferrari ran a higher-than-ideal inflation pressure on the first set of tyres during the race. That was not a mistake as such, but a deliberate attempt to get the tyres up to temperature more quickly, a call that backfired.

The higher internal pressure reduced the contact patch between tyre and tarmac, which progressively increased the temperature in the tread and accelerated degradation.

All the cars were sliding laterally because of the low grip levels, with the rear tyres also showing pronounced spinning.

Reduced downforce, through lower wing angles, combined with slightly higher ride heights than would be used in dry conditions, led to considerably faster tyre wear that was not offset by the car getting lighter as fuel burned off.

The São Paulo Grand Prix laid bare just how narrow Ferrari's performance window really is. To compensate for the power unit's shortfall, the car's overall balance, and crucially the correct management of the tyres, was effectively sacrificed, independent of the decisions Lewis Hamilton made on track against the instructions coming from his own pit wall.

title: Isack Hadjar told of 'next step' with Red Bull in face of Max Verstappen challenge
excerpt:
Red Bull technical director Pierre Waché has outlined winning races as the "next step" for Isack Hadjar, albeit acknowledging the scale of the task the Frenchman faces in trying to match Max Verstappen.

Hadjar has scored three podiums in his first season alongside Verstappen; in Monaco, Baku and most recently in São Paulo, where he finished third after running second and yielding position to the four-time F1 champion under team orders.

Red Bull has already rewarded that progress, extending Hadjar's contract through 2027 on the back of regular top-six finishes and qualifying pace increasingly close to that of Verstappen.

It is a marked turnaround from the recent history of Red Bull's second seat, which proved brutally unforgiving for both Pierre Gasly and Alexander Albon, before each rebuilt their reputations elsewhere on the grid, as well as Liam Lawson.

Speaking to RacingNews365, Waché explained that Hadjar's development has been built on communication with his side of the garage as much as raw speed.

"First, he has to contribute for himself, to say what he needs to go quick," said Waché. "He has improved a lot since the start of the season. He clearly has pace in him, like we have seen.

"When you have a new engineer or a new driver, you have to get to know each other. You have to understand the vocabulary used for the needs he has.

"But he's developing well. He has massive potential in him, and a desire to win. That is what we are looking for.

"We need a second driver to be very good in the constructors' championship. That is our aim.

"He is in the right place, and he is the future of the team, otherwise we would not have taken him."

[Article continues below]

Asked whether Hadjar is delivering in the way Red Bull hoped from its second driver, having gone through several difficult pairings in recent years, Waché was reluctant to dwell on the past.

"I don't want to look at that," he said. "Maybe it was difficult, and maybe it was our fault.

"At the moment, he is doing exactly what we need. To be honest, he is challenging the system; he is at the right position."

Pushed on what comes next after Hadjar's run of podium finishes, the technical director set out a clear marker.

"The next step will be to win races and everything, but he has his desire," said Waché. "He's developing, and to be fair with him, it's a tough job to be against the best driver."

title: Former Ferrari F1 hopeful completes 'demanding' Lola Formula E switch
excerpt:
Former Ferrari junior driver Robert Shwartzman has signed for Lola as the team's first driver for the Gen4 era of the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship.

The Israeli-born driver brings a varied résumé to his Formula E debut. Shwartzman won the 2019 Formula 3 title with three victories and 10 podiums before stepping up to Formula 2, where he finished runner-up in 2021.

He later took on reserve and development duties in Formula 1 for Ferrari, picked up a maiden World Endurance Championship win at Lone Star Le Mans in 2024, and made headlines by claiming pole position for the 2025 Indianapolis 500 as a rookie.

Although it will be his first full Formula E campaign, Shwartzman has already completed rookie tests and free practice outings in the series. Alongside his Lola deal, he is also set to compete in the 2027 FIA WEC season for Peugeot.

The 26-year-old has been putting in laps in the Lola T004 during testing, working closely with the Huntingdon-based squad and technical partner Yamaha.

The Japanese manufacturer is continuing to partner with Lola on development of the Gen4 powertrain, bringing its engineering expertise to the championship's next-generation technology ahead of the 2027 season.

Shwartzman set for double 2027 racing programme

Shwartzman is a driver who has been linked with a seat in Formula E for a couple of seasons, and was spotted with Lola earlier this year in Berlin.

He has not conducted a racing programme in 2026 but will race in both Formula E and WEC in 2027, a challenge he is wary will be "demanding".

"I'm very excited to join the Formula E grid and start this new chapter of my career with Lola," he said. "Formula E is such a competitive, unique championship and one I've wanted to race in for a long time.

"Balancing my commitments between WEC and Formula E is going to make for a demanding, non-stop season but honestly, after not racing in 2026, I missed it so much. Being back to doing what I love most, especially with a double campaign across two world class programmes, is an incredible feeling. I'm really grateful to everyone who worked behind the scenes to give me this opportunity.

"What makes joining this project so special is working with a legendary name like Lola as we enter the Gen4 era. The Gen4 car is an absolute beast and so much fun to drive, I really can't wait to start the season and push it to the limit on what looks like a fantastic calendar."

Lola team principal Mark Preston said the team was delighted to bring the former Ferrari junior on board.

"Robert's results and experience speak for themselves, and we are so pleased to be welcoming him to Lola Formula E," Preston said.

"While he enters the series as a rookie facing a genuine learning curve against established grid veterans, his proven ability to adapt quickly across different categories makes him a highly promising prospect for the Gen4 era.

"He has already shown strong potential behind the wheel and has integrated well into the team, providing invaluable feedback as we prepare for the 2027 season."

title: Lewis Hamilton backed to still be on F1 grid in 2030 and fulfil Africa dream
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has what it takes to still be racing in Formula 1 in 2030.

That's the verdict of a RacingNews365 poll regarding the seven-time F1 champion's longevity in the sport, and whether he will be around at the start of the next decade when an African GP draws near.

Of those who took part, 47.89 per cent backed Hamilton to still be on the grid in four years, while 26.84 per cent said it was too early to tell, pointing to 2027 and 2028 as the seasons that will make things clearer. The remaining 25.26 per cent felt Hamilton should not be targeting a career that long.

The poll follows weeks of Hamilton himself fuelling speculation about extending his Ferrari career, with the Briton's current deal running through 2027 and reports suggesting it carries options into 2028. Hamilton has pointed to Formula 1's planned return to Africa, via a prospective Rwanda race, as a personal motivation to keep going.

"I'm now forced to have to stay longer because we have a race in Africa; that's been my dream to be able to race in Africa," Hamilton said after a race in Rwanda was confirmed recently.

"I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

Hamilton also pushed back on suggestions that age will inevitably slow him down, indicating he feels uniquely placed among his peers.

"You've never had anyone like me here in the 70 years [of F1]," said Hamilton. "I feel that I'm built differently. There have been so many preconceived ideas about the fact that your reaction time drops off.

"I can't say in four years whether I want to continue to do what I'm doing, but I love what I'm doing still now.

"Whether or not I can compete at 44 with a 20-year-old, who knows? But at 41, I can compete with a 20-year-old. So time will tell."

title: Kimi Antonelli handed verdict over future Ferrari drive: 'He could go tomorrow'
excerpt:
Guenther Steiner has no doubt Kimi Antonelli will one day drive for Ferrari.

Incoming F1 champion Antonelli is contracted to the Brackley-based squad until at least the end of 2027 after the team exercised an option on his deal. Despite enjoying a flying start to the season, though, Mercedes' dominance has slipped of late.

Naturally, given Antonelli's Italian heritage, and the fact Ferrari is approaching two decades since its last drivers' champion, there has been speculation over a longer-term move to Ferrari.

Former Haas team principal Steiner sees it as a matter of when, rather than if, the 20-year-old will one day drive for the Scuderia.

Asked whether he could envisage Antonelli at Ferrari, speaking to RacingNews365, Italian Steiner replied: "Some people ask why he is not driving for us. That's the only not-so-perfect thing for Italy, that there is an Italian champion not driving for Ferrari.

"But I think at some stage. Think about it. He's 20 years old. He's so young, so at some stage, in my opinion, he will drive for Ferrari.

"Will it be short term? No. It will be maybe 10 years out. But at some stage, obviously, as an Italian with this talent, he will get there.

"I would turn it around. They will get him. He could go tomorrow if he wants."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli in 'right place at right time'

Steiner, who has expressed pride in Antonelli's achieve, has also suggested his ascension this year could mark the beginning of a dominant period for the youngster, pointing to the timing of his arrival alongside F1's new technical rules.

Asked if this could be the start of an era for the Italian, Steiner said: "Yes. He's there the first year of these new regulations.

"In motorsport, especially F1, you need to be at the right place at the right time, and he's hit that - he's at the right place at the right time.

"But Mercedes, with these regulations, are very strong. They are not dominating, which is good for everybody.

"It means he cannot be told 'Just win, because you have got the best machine'.

"No, he wins because he's got a good machine and he's the best at the moment, but I'm pretty sure he will win a few more world championships."

title: FIA called to intervene after Lando Norris injury near-miss: 'He's very lucky'
excerpt:
David Coulthard has called on the FIA to review its podium safety procedures after Lando Norris once again smashed a champagne bottle against the floor during his São Paulo Grand Prix celebrations, warning that the McLaren driver was "very lucky" to escape injury.

Norris sealed a dominant win at Interlagos, surviving changeable conditions that forced multiple tyre switches across the 71-lap race.

But his post-race celebrations once again saw him slam a bottle hard enough to shatter it, echoing a similar incident at Monza in 2020 that left him with cuts to his hand.

The 2025 world champion's podium trouble was not solely smashing his champagne bottle, as he followed it up by accidentally putting his face into the pyrotechnic sparks.

Coulthard, speaking on the Up to Speed podcast, said the Briton needs to break the habit before it causes serious harm.

"I was really impressed across the board, with some standout performances," Coulthard said. "The obvious one is Lando, absolutely brilliant. Although we have to address right at the top that he's got to stop doing the same thing and expecting a different outcome.

"Banging the bottle, like right here, kids, banging glass on anything is not a good idea. You teach your smallest of children not to do that, and yet he continues to do it. He's very lucky.

"In all seriousness, he hasn't, like, gashed his hand. The FIA obviously needs to have a little look at the podium and do a little sense check on anything that could sparkle its way into the eye of a driver. So there's the first thing that needs a rework."

Lando Norris Brazil victory 'one of his best drives'

Despite his concerns over the celebration, Coulthard was unequivocal in his praise for the drive that preceded it, with Norris managing the switch between intermediate tyres and slicks as rain returned late in the race to threaten his lead.

"It was world-class," Coulthard added. "It was one of his best drives ever. It was awesome because of the nature of that track and the changing conditions, just absolutely phenomenal.

"We're in a wonderful era of Formula 1, where we've got a number of world-class drivers who, given the moment, the car and the confidence, have all got a chance of getting out there and mixing it up."

"Rather worryingly, I guess, for Lando and the other guys, is Max coming from the back to finish second with a car that he was far from happy with, which again is just remarkable."
